Details: Communist organizers build national pressure while contesting control of individual states. The root event immediately seeds one Level 1 controlled state so the player sees the map layer and response decisions right away. The national spirit gives a small daily communist drift, and each communist-controlled state adds +0.01 daily communist support through dynamic pressure. States progress through Agitation Zone, Insurgent Stronghold, and Communist Lockdown levels; Level 3 creates a demilitarized revolutionary lockdown zone. Local military intervention works only on Levels 1-2; Disrupt Communist Organizing reduces national communist support; emergency national intervention affects all controlled states and can trigger a custom rebel country without vanilla stockpile splitting. Once controlled states are gone, rebels are not active, and communist support falls below the spread threshold. World Revolution stays locked until Whispers of the World Revolution is reached.
Evo I: Gathering Storm: Unstable Revolutionary Activity begins once any state is communist-controlled. Enables rare surprise revolts, including very rare one-state breakaway revolts with rebel armies scaled by state and country strength.
Evo II: Rising Chaos: Dark Worker Rituals begins once a Level 2 stronghold exists. Enables rare worker ritual incidents that disrupt a controlled state, raise intervention risk, improve later conversion chance, and slightly increase communist support.
Evo III: Chaos Tier: Whispers of the World Revolution begins once a Level 3 lockdown exists. Unlocks World Revolution for the major-event pool. Later whisper events add 200 World Revolution weight and mark states as more likely to join uprisings.
World-End Scenario: No terminal world-end. Whispers of the World Revolution hands the communist crisis to the separate World Revolution major event, where controlled states may become revolutionary bases.

Details:
The outbreak begins in one random populous state. Zombies use only manpower for their divisions, and thus depend a lot on the population of states they capture. If the horde gets momentum, it spreads fast and captured land is cored right away.

Secondary outbreaks happen most likely in big, crowded, less developed states. Chaos makes those outbreaks more common over time, and each zombie evolution makes the horde harder to contain.

If you want to keep the event under control, the main things that matter are holding the front, cutting outbreak risk with prevention decisions, pushing cure research, and joining the Anti-Zombie League.
Evo I: Gathering Storm: the first major zombie adaptation makes the horde much harder to starve out and much stronger at night. It is the point where early containment starts slipping, and cure work begins getting harder.
Evo II: Rising Chaos: the horde turns into a faster assault force with better attack pressure and even less reliance on supply. Finding the cure becomes harder again.
Evo III: Chaos Tier: weak fronts can collapse fast, and the cure is at its hardest to finish.
World-End Scenario:
Zombie Apocalypse

The outbreak has outgrown every line built to contain it. The dead move from ruined cities into the last organized refuges, while the living lose the roads, laboratories, and armies needed to answer them.

The Zombie Horde becomes the dominant order of the world. Isolated survivors remain in scattered refuges under a world ordered by the dead.

Details: Transforms Tibet or a Tibet-centered Himalayan state into the Holy Realm. The route begins as a defensive mountain refuge, develops into a Bodhisattva-led state, creates the Arhat Administration, reaches the Buddha Mandate, and can branch into restraint, peacekeeping, coercive pacification, Divine Sovereignty, or the final doctrine. Evolutions are focus-path gates; the actual mechanics come from the selected focuses, decisions, and events inside those unlocked paths.
Evo I: Mountain Refuge: forms The Holy Realm, initializes Mandala and Buddhahood counters, applies fragile refuge ideas, opens the Mandala GUI/category, loads the focus tree, and starts shelter, road, refugee, early teaching, and defensive play.
Evo II: Bodhisattva Teaching and Meditation: Send Dhamma Envoys, Guard the Pilgrimage Route, Translate the Wheel, teaching-under-fire, and the concentration-vow sequence raise Bodhi, Compassion, Dhyana Depth, and Meditation Charge while tracking clean-route and Defilement risks.
Evo III: Governance, Sanctuary, Guardian, and Sangha Compact routes: Council/Regent/Assembly choices, infrastructure and supply works, Temple Guard and pilgrimage escort systems, compact admission, aid, anti-puppet clauses, and AI weights support defensive humanitarian play against special chaos countries.
Evo IV: The Unshaken Seat and Powers: Buddhahood requires 108 Bodhi, Fourth Dhyana, low Defilements, teaching successes, crisis teaching, and the focus marker. Success changes leader/stage, fires The Awakened One, unlocks the Buddha powers category, and the first anti-chaos power display fires Powers of the Awakened.
Evo V: Final Silence and Schism: the hidden False Buddha branch supports debate, exile, suppression, and absorption outcomes. Extinction of Defilements, Witnesses Gather, and the final doctrine balance gate non-terminal Empty Seat aftermath versus terminal Final Silence.
World-End Scenario:
The Final Silence

The Holy Realm carries its last doctrine into firing tables, distant commands, and the machinery of war. Its arsenals serve a single purpose: silence.

The Empty Seat's final order silences organized resistance and ordinary state life. Radio networks, armies, and governments disappear into a world that has fallen quiet.

Details: A random eligible country declares war on another eligible country. Higher chaos stages create larger linked war webs. Compatible special countries can appear in later stages.
Evo I: Gathering Storm: Triangular Incident. Three declarations fire in one linked dispute.
Evo II: Rising Chaos: Four Fronts. Four declarations fire in one conflict web, with a small chance for a compatible special country to appear.
Evo III: Chaos Tier: Contagious Ultimatums. Five declarations fire, major countries and faction members become more likely, and special-country involvement becomes more common.
Evo IV: Totalen Chaos: The War Week. Six declarations fire in a short chain, with a strong chance of one compatible special country participating.
Evo V: World Collapse: Open Season. Seven to eight declarations fire while normal random events still run. Compatible special countries are strongly favored when available.

Details:
The Soviet Union is losing command over its republics, rail offices, garrisons, and depots. Moscow can answer with force, negotiation, isolation, or party discipline, but each visible failure gives local authorities more room to act.

Forced-labor quotas, grain extraction, and NKVD campaigns can briefly reinforce Moscow's authority, but each use deepens famine pressure, republic fear, old-movement grievance, and the evidence record. Once the crisis becomes severe, repression can no longer reduce the terminal threat.

Breakaway republics can seek recognition, seize depots, coordinate defenses, or draw more republics into the crisis while Moscow tries to restore command or force a new settlement.
Evo I: First Durable Secession: a republic ministry, garrison, or depot network stops obeying Moscow and survives long enough to make its break visible.
Evo II: Regional Cascade: several republics are free, and release pressure spreads through foreign attention, depot weakness, League coordination, and public refusal.
Evo III: Union Unmade: Moscow has lost Union-wide command. Remaining ordinary republics are forced out of the old center, and the former Union enters open war over its borders.
Evo IV: Maximum Rupture: every remaining republic and eligible special splinter can break from the former Union. The crisis becomes a map-wide struggle over who inherits the old state.
Evo V: World Collapse Rupture: the same break reaches its final intensity, forcing the last eligible remnants into the open while the former Union becomes one front among a collapsing world.

Details: Across several regions, provisional states rise in one synchronized wave from viable local claims, prepared institutions, regional identities, and remembered polities. Automatic waves release 6 countries in Calm World, 8 in Gathering Storm, 10 in Rising Chaos, 14 in Chaos Tier, and 20 in Totalen Chaos. World Collapse also releases 20 while raising force, instability, rarity, and ambition pressure. Their former hosts retain a remnant, but the new governments inherit unsettled borders, disputed assets, fragile forces, and urgent struggles for recognition. The crisis opens at stability below 35%, an enemy-controlled owned state above 50 resistance, or a controlled foreign-owned state above 50 resistance. The 120-day crisis queues the ordinary doubled wave when pressure remains. A busy coordinator uses a bounded retry, while an invalid or exhausted plan fails closed without changing ownership. Each new country must choose how to govern, secure itself, bargain with its former host, and resist or accept competing patrons.
Evo I:
The Manuals Cross the Border

Founding charters, civil-service manuals, recognition protocols, and trusted couriers now pass from one young state to the next. New governments enter the world with stronger institutions, earlier diplomatic contacts, and a network prepared to sponsor their survival.
Evo II:
Old Nations Wake

Dormant national projects and half-remembered unions return to political life. Regional and signature independence movements can surface sooner, while the states already born from the wave gain the confidence and institutions needed to rediscover larger identities.
Evo III:
Flags Rise Behind the Barracks

The next declarations arrive with officers, guarded depots, and plans for immediate defense. Breakaway governments gain stronger military budgets and better prepared forces, but every rifle issued sharpens instability, former-host hostility, and the fear of reconquest.
Evo IV:
The Sovereigns Take Their Seats

The informal network becomes a congress of delegates, observers, and rejected clients. Recognition missions, arbitration, rescue commitments, and a shared reserve draw the independent states toward collective leadership without deciding the charter they must ultimately choose.
Evo V:
No Border Is Final

World collapse strips old borders of their final authority. New sovereignty projects enter the struggle for independence, while existing breakaways gain the freedom and pressure to pursue dangerous routes.

Details: Fury turns an eligible non-player minor country into an expansionist war state while keeping the player, subjects, majors, player-linked countries, and island-only countries out of the selection pool. The actor receives the Fury Column template, stockpiles scaled to its size, recurring reinforcement waves, War Office decisions, and a shared focus tree. Fury seeks valid neighboring targets, records its first conquest, and escalates through Hardened Fury, second-actor cooperation or rivalry, all-border pressure, and world-end containment.
Evo I: Hardened Fury: unlocks once the first Fury cycle escalates. Future and eligible current Fury actors receive the hardened national spirit, more starting columns, higher momentum, and a stronger sustained reinforcement profile.
Evo II: Second War Table: ensures at least two Fury actors can exist, unlocks cooperation and rivalry content, enables Fury Pact handling, and records the second evolution in the event log.
Evo III: All Borders Burn: ensures up to three Fury actors, strengthens weekly growth, allows all-border declarations, and unlocks the world-end candidate focus path.
World-End Scenario:
The World in Fury

Fury is no longer confined to one rogue state. Armed hosts answer one another across continents, each treating the nearest border as an invitation to attack and every pause as weakness.

A network of Fury states opens a global war without a negotiated political end. Rage becomes the world's governing order.

Details: Tensions Rising is a repeatable diplomatic-pressure incident. In calm conditions it adds world tension and stops once world tension is full. At higher chaos levels it can still fire at maximum world tension, adding direct chaos increase, indirect pressure through timer pacing, timed opinion penalties, AI readiness ideas, and delayed reports.
Evo I: Cable Traffic Increase. The first evolved stage moves the incident beyond a simple world-tension increase. Relation shocks begin, and later incidents can briefly gather pace.
Evo II: Competing Accusations. The second stage reaches more capitals. Timed relation damage can affect additional pairs, delayed reports become more likely, and some governments take short-lived readiness postures.
Evo III: Staff Readiness. The third stage treats the pattern as a planning concern. Relation shocks last longer, diplomatic aftershocks remain temporary, and peaceful players can begin the Thin Wire watch while world tension remains full.
Evo IV: Extended Alert. The fourth stage is the strongest non-terminal form of the incident. It keeps pressure indirect and does not create a direct conflict branch.

Details:
White Peace searches for wars that can end without conquest, indemnity, or scripted-story damage. At first it settles one minor country pair under the same flags and the same borders.

Later evolutions can settle several minor pairs, rarely include a major country, or issue broader diplomatic settlements when the world has too many wars.

Its selection weight rises with active wars and valid minor-war candidates, but repeated firings and higher evolutions keep it from becoming common.
Evo I: Repeated Minor Settlements: Repeated Minor Settlements lets one firing quiet several minor fronts when enough safe pairs exist.
Evo II: Major-Country Settlement: Major-Country Settlement allows a rare no-gain exit involving a major country when the war segment can be settled without rewriting the wider conflict.
Evo III: Broad Diplomatic Settlement: Broad Diplomatic Settlement lets one armistice circular quiet broader safe war clutter while leaving protected wars untouched.

Details:
Death is a hidden island crisis that can become a war. It begins by taking one remote island and waiting in silence. Before the public reveal, island spread looks for small island states, especially nearby islands under 100K people, before widening to other low-population island targets.

When Death consumes a state, the state is not occupied in the normal way. Its full population is removed and recorded in the Deaths System, then the state is transferred to Death, cored by Death, stripped of factories, dockyards, ports, infrastructure, and other usable buildings, and marked with the active wasteland modifier. Local manpower, factories, resources, supply, and movement are ruined there. Units caught inside are withered, and recaptured wastelands stay dangerous until countries invest in recovery work.

Death grows through the Black Ledger. Each consumed state adds soul power, and consumed population adds more at one soul power per 250K people. After the world-end stage begins, last-shore footholds add extra soul power as well. Available soul power is what Death has generated but not yet spent.

Death spends soul power on forced island spread, mainland pressure, and ghost hosts. Early hosts are weak and passive, later hosts become stronger, and the world-end stage lets Death open last-shore footholds on surviving continents.

Living countries answer through investigation decisions, early survey boats, war declarations after the danger is clearer, coastal watches, quarantine lines, the Living Compact, wasteland entry gear, dead-zone outposts, and risky Black Book methods. Defeating Death means retaking every state it controls.
Evo I: Second Shore: Death can unlock its first island-spread focus path. It can begin taking more low-population islands, but the pace remains slow and the mainland route stays closed.
Evo II: Mainland Hunger: Death can press the island pattern faster and unlock the mainland focus path. A valid coastal mainland state can become the public reveal point once enough island pressure exists.
Evo III: First Hosts: Near the 600 chaos mark, Death can gain weak custom ghost divisions with very low organization. They hold borders passively and are much weaker than infantry.
Evo IV: Hollow Hosts: Near the 800 chaos mark, Death can gain more custom ghost divisions with higher organization and strength. They remain weaker than infantry and should still be pushable.
Evo V: World End: Once Death has consumed a full continent and Chaos is above 1000, Death gains many infantry-parity hosts and begins attacking aggressively.
World-End Scenario:
Last Shores

Death has emptied enough land to turn islands, wastelands, and ghost hosts into one design. A consumed continent gives Zol the ground from which to reach every surviving shore.

New footholds open across the living world, and the dead march from the last shores to complete the Black Ledger. No population remains beyond Death's count.

Details: Foreign meetings, missing couriers, damaged equipment, and repeated methods form an uneasy pattern around the country. Investigation can connect the incidents while practical safeguards reduce their effect.
Evo I: Reports from distant regions repeat the same routes, methods, and timings. Leaks and defections can expose links without identifying every government involved.
Evo II: The pattern supports a credible case of organized foreign interference. Serious covert action is possible, and the target can build suspect confidence, independent Evidence, and maintained Preparedness.
Evo III: Military precautions, public warnings, and border pressure indicate that the hidden crisis is nearing an open confrontation. Preparation and preemption can still alter the opening.
World-End Scenario: None. Event 011 may become an open coalition war, but it has no world-end branch.

Details: Reserved

Warnings arrive from named states as rivers leave their banks, faults break, storms cross transport belts, ash buries fields, and fires outrun the roads. Local reports follow each impact into rescue, stabilization, and reconstruction while nearby states watch for the danger to spread.
Evo I:
Wider Disaster Seasons

Disaster seasons carry more impacts and a broader family pool. Warning choices and family reports remain local, while repeated hits make rescue and stabilization capacity harder to allocate.

Chaos Tier: Gathering Storm
Evolution Stage: Wider Disaster Seasons
Evo II:
Regional Cascades

Deaths and damage rise sharply. Neighboring states suffer transport and supply disruption. Famine, disease, refugee pressure, delayed deaths, and reconstruction strain become central risks when recovery falters.

Chaos Tier: Rising Chaos
Evolution Stage: Regional Cascades
Evo III:
Abnormal Paths

Abnormal disasters can travel across regions as rupture waves, meteor showers, eruption plumes, storm corridors, tornado tracks, and tsunami paths. The abnormal map shows queued danger and the places likely to be struck next.

Chaos Tier: Chaos
Evolution Stage: Abnormal Paths
World-End Scenario: None. Evolution III permits devastating abnormal disaster paths but remains non-terminal.

Details:
Cannibalism begins with evidence recovered from an army at war. Burial parties vanish, ration ledgers are altered, and isolated formations report deliberate cutting and predation within their own ranks. Scarcity may explain the first crimes, but repeated methods suggest that damaged commands are protecting the perpetrators.

The crisis tests whether military institutions can restore supply, protect witnesses and the dead, and distinguish frightened soldiers from organized killers. Concealment may preserve calm while allowing the pattern to survive. Public terror may hold a front while teaching other units that predation brings rank and protection.
Evo I:
Ritualized Ranks

Scattered predation has become a shared ideology of oaths, marks, promotion, and protected membership. No shared headquarters appears in the records.
Evo II:
The Organized Network

Cells in separate countries use matching ledgers, routes, prisoner practices, and operational timing. Captured records identify no common headquarters.
Evo III:
Hannibal Lecter Commands

The concealed command is publicly revealed, and the mature network begins unification under Hannibal Lecter.
World-End Scenario:
The World Is the Larder

Lecter's host has joined scattered feeding territories and armed kitchens into one command. Roads, farms, prisons, and conquered cities are treated as parts of a single larder, with surviving states left as prey or resistance enclaves.

Organized consumption becomes a permanent world order. Every surviving government faces the same expanding host, and the network no longer has any reason to hide.

No Thaw Will Come

Lecter's winter host has surrendered its last human restraints to the Wendigo form. Feeding grounds spread with the cold, and conquered communities are folded into a hunger that treats thaw, harvest, and mercy as weaknesses.

An advancing winter covers the world. The Wendigo command pursues every surviving country until organized human rule is consumed or driven into isolated refuges.

Details:
A translated manifesto passes from reading rooms into the ministries of a small country. It proposes that public need should govern common stores, useful work, settlements, and the obligations of citizenship. Its readers disagree over whether freedom is secured by consent, shared councils, expert measure, disciplined separation, or the right to revise the book itself.

As the experiment takes hold, shortages, public works, local charters, and agreements with neighboring states test every interpretation. Promises are judged through visible provision and conduct, while each territorial case asks whether necessity can cross a border without becoming appetite.
Evo I:
Glosses in the Margin

The recovered manuscript no longer speaks with one voice. Rival translations, household annotations, and public commentaries have become organized schools of interpretation. Delegates arrive carrying copies marked by workshops, parishes, councils, and exiles. The argument over the book has become an institution of its own, and the eventual commonwealth will be shaped by whoever keeps the right to write in its margins.
Evo II:
Necessary Shores

Migration, blockade, crowded housing, and uncertain supply have pushed the common store against the limits of the map. Surveyors now distinguish want from ambition before they mark a harbor, corridor, settlement, or lease as necessary ground. Domestic works remain possible, and every foreign offer leaves a record. The experiment must decide whether need can cross a border without turning into appetite.
Evo III:
Cities of One Measure

The settlement plan has escaped the capital. Cooperative municipalities, associated towns, and rebuilt districts repeat its gardens, clinics, workshops, stores, and transport links in different soil. Each place adapts the design to local votes and local shortages. Their growing network makes the manifesto visible in ordinary streets, while disputes over assignment reveal who is allowed to alter the plan.
Evo IV:
Nowhere Made Law

The manifesto has become a regional legal identity. Governments and movements invoke it when they negotiate association, refuse an ultimatum, request aid, or defend local charters. Sponsors offer protection with conditions, rivals describe every storehouse as a disguised frontier, and small states judge whether the commonwealth is refuge, partner, or threat. An imagined country has become a claim that diplomacy must answer.
Evo V:
The Perfect Island

Ordinary regional order is breaking around a society trying to make one bounded place endure. Reserve trains, guarded harbors, refugee districts, fortification works, and member councils all pull against one another. The closed route hardens the boundary through compulsory service and carries the cost inside its gates. The voluntary route distributes refuge among willing towns and spreads the obligation across its members. Stores must remain open as the roads beyond them fail.

Details: Random country gets a brilliant scientist which grants 100% faster research speed

An independent minor outside the factions is cornered by the blocs able to offer membership and forced to choose one. A player country caught in the decision receives up to four faction offers and must sign with one of them.

The accession unsettles nearby neutral capitals, gives faction leaders a reason to court the border, and turns neutrality into work that has to be defended in public, in councils, and at frontier posts.
Evo I:
Regional Bloc Race

Regional pressure starts spreading from one accession to neighboring neutrals. Border posts, observer invitations, neutrality councils, and faction staff missions become the public tools of the race.
Evo II:
Pressured Neutrality

War draws neutral cabinets into the faction struggle. Countries beside active fronts face sharper demands, and faction leaders press exposed capitals for public commitments.
Evo III:
Collapse of Neutrality

Several small states in one region can be drawn toward rival blocs in quick succession. Some capitals still try to hold their line through hurried councils, guarded borders, and costly declarations of neutrality.

Details: Surveyors in an owned state discover a major strategic resource deposit. Repeated discoveries can deepen the same field, turning local prospecting into a long-lived question of development, labor, trade, and control.
Evo I: Veins Without End: One field reveals several large deposits at once. Repeated finds of the same resource deepen its discovery ledger, while foreign buyers, claimants, and a negotiated demilitarized commission compete for access to the concentrated wealth.
Evo II: The Workings Turn Sick: Sickness, corrosion, disappearances, and underground attacks spread through the lower workings. Investigation, containment, concealment, suspension, and permanent closure determine whether the field remains an economy or becomes a grave.
Evo III: The Breach Takes Shape: A vast deposit of every standard resource draws the field far below safe workings. Public attacks, hunts, evacuation, partial closure, and a full sealing operation decide whether every registered discovery deposit is surrendered before the breach opens.
Evo IV: The Oth-Kesh Emerge: The field becomes the origin chamber of the playable Oth-Kesh Host. Its armored broods draw strength from exploitation and captured resource anchors, attack every adjacent land neighbor, and prepare to carry the connected depths beyond their first continent.
World-End Scenario:
The World Opens Below

The Oth-Kesh Host has secured its first continent and prepared resource-rich ruptures beyond it. The chambers below the surface become roads, and the deep war crosses the seas through new footholds.

Every surviving continent faces a local Oth-Kesh front tied to the World Below. The surface becomes one global war against the world beneath it.

Details: Across the world, fully formed military units begin appearing without recruitment orders, training records, or a known source. Governments register, equip, command, and contain soldiers who arrived already organized. When anomalous hosts enter the rolls, their first delegations demand a choice between cantonment, negotiated autonomy, and refusal. Claimants and claimant-free hosts can later carry their recorded formations into rival commands.
Evo I: Organized Muster: The unbidden formations have been placed under district staffs, common rolls, and an accountable chain of command.
Evo II: Arsenal Lottery: New formations arrive with strange equipment packages that demand separate training, repair, and supply arrangements.
Evo III: Command Fracture: Randomly assembled formations now produce commanders whose private authority can rival the state.
Evo IV: Anomalous Muster: Recognized nonhuman hosts can appear among the formations, bringing distinct obligations, containment needs, and the danger of armed secession.

The Children's Ward Report

The children's ward in [?fallout_event_175_triage_state_id.GetName] received enough medicine to prevent the worst cases, but two outer rooms waited through the coldest night. The surviving families can see where the list narrowed.

The Workshop Ward Report

The workshop ward in [?fallout_event_175_triage_state_id.GetName] saved enough workers to keep one route open. The outer salvage teams still lost hours to fever, so the production ledger shows a recovery with a cost.

The workshop ward in [?fallout_event_175_triage_state_id.GetName] could not return its crews to the cold depots. The Deaths register and the broken equipment list now share a column, and the clinic faces the families of the missing workers.
Evo III:
The Guard Ward Report

The guard ward in [?fallout_event_175_triage_state_id.GetName] returned patrol leaders and stretcher teams to duty. Their officers accepted the clinic's order, and [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentOfficial] can protect the next convoy without stripping the shelters bare.

The guard ward in [?fallout_event_175_triage_state_id.GetName] lost too many soldiers to rebuild the patrol roster. The Deaths register reaches the barracks, while [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentAuthority] must answer for a choice that left both guards and civilians afraid.

Event Name: The Archive Above the Rail Cut
Details: A cold store survived beneath the old freight embankment. Its drawers hold seed envelopes, field notes, and a ledger that names three districts which still have hands to plant. The archive cannot serve every claimant. The council must decide whether seed is a state reserve, a farmer's trust, a promise between countries, or a thing sold to whoever can pay.
Evo I:
The State Seed Ledger

The public reserve opened under a single ledger. Clerks from the rail cut counted every envelope, while the first protected plots received water before the next frost.

The archive was catalogued, but two drawers had already taken damp. The remaining packets can reach the fields if the reclamation crews keep the route open.

The state seal arrived before the drying racks. Mold and hurried hands ruined part of the archive, and the shelter wards recorded the cost of the lost planting season.
Evo II:
The Farmers' Covenant

The field cooperatives accepted the archive under a public covenant. Their first plots follow the sheltered drainage lines, and the seed keepers have written down which families carry each variety.

The cooperatives saved a planting schedule, but the cold ground forced them to choose only the safest plots. The covenant now carries a debt to the families left outside the first allotment.

The archive reached the fields without enough sheltered ground. The first planting failed, and families who were promised a share now remember the covenant as a broken law.
Evo III:
Packets Across the Waterline

The first packets crossed the waterline with a clean-water convoy. The allied delegates recorded the exchange in both ledgers, giving the archive a route beyond one damaged country.

Some packets crossed, but the convoy arrived with less water than promised. The exchange remains visible in both ledgers and the next shipment will be argued over.

The exchange collapsed at the checkpoint. The archive lost a season of water testing, and the partner's delegates now treat the seed offer as another broken promise.
Evo IV:
A Price on the First Green

Licensed buyers paid in scrap and transport hours. The archive gained a working route to the fields, although every receipt now carries the names of those who could not bid.

The auction paid for part of the route, but the highest bids came from the same districts that already held the safest ground. The public ledger records both the food and the resentment.

The auction drew promises instead of transport. The packets were delayed, the reclamation crews lost their window, and the shelters counted another season without a reliable crop.
Evo V:
The First Harvest Review

The agronomist returned with envelopes from the first protected plots. The archive now has a living charter, and the state can name which route carried each successful variety.

The review found a usable harvest, but not a common rule. The archive remains open while each district argues over the next packet and the cost of keeping it dry.

The review found no safe harvest to certify. The archive will remain a warning in the state memory, with access grievance attached to every future seed debate.

The old greenhouse district kept three sealed crates through the Air Winter. The first leaves are alive, but their veins are mottled and the planting ledger names no safe answer. The food council must decide whether to destroy the batch, risk a full planting, keep it behind filters, or send samples to growers who can judge it beyond this state.
Evo I:
Ash on the Burn Pits

The medicine stores kept the burn crews sealed while scrap-fed furnaces reduced every crate to black husk. The river district lost a tempting harvest, but no mottled leaf reached the public beds.

The council destroyed the worst crates and saved a dry packet for comparison. The quarantine held in the rail district, although the next planting now depends on a smaller reserve.

The burn team opened a cracked crate without a second filter. Spores crossed the work yard before the furnace caught, and the southern plots now carry a crop warning beside the hospital tents.
Evo II:
The First Greenhouse Furrows

The food compact planted every sheltered furrow before the thaw line broke. The leaves held their color, and the district ledger now names a cultivar that can feed the next ration cycle.

The planting crews chose the warmest beds and left the rest covered. Some rows took root, but the settlement will have to ration seed while the outer farms wait for a cleaner reading.

The first leaves curled after the thaw. The greenhouse walls trapped a gray blight, and the eastern shelter has lost both a season of food and the confidence to open its seed store.
Evo III:
Filters Around the Trial Beds

The shelter engineers sealed four trial beds behind clean filters and logged every hand that crossed the airlock. The hill capital can compare the leaves without exposing the public allotments.

The filter wall held around the best beds, but one service tunnel stayed open during the coldest week. The trial survives with a narrow harvest and a debt to the crews who kept watch.

The replacement filters arrived after the first inspection. Dust entered the trial chamber, workers fell ill, and the valley farms now carry a blight marker while the council closes its doors.
Evo IV:
Packets Across the Ash Road

Partner growers received the samples in sealed tins and returned a planting note from the coast. The exchange gives the food compact a second reading and a route toward a cultivar that can cross the ash road.

The samples reached one cooperative, while the second convoy turned back at the burned bridge. The council gained a useful comparison, but the missing reply leaves the inland plots waiting.

The sample tins arrived without a clean chain of custody. The partner growers rejected the batch, the recognition ledger fell, and the greenhouse council must answer for a promise made too soon.
Evo V:
The Cultivar Review

The delayed review compared the greenhouse leaves with the ash-road notes. The state can now name a stable cultivar and assign its first beds without reopening the original hazard.

The review found a usable line, but the evidence remains divided between the shelter wall and the partner farms. The next planting will carry a public warning and a narrow license.

The final samples failed the review. The batch remains a memory of rushed hunger, and the state marks the old greenhouse as a closed hazard until a cleaner generation can test it.

The Sealed Levels Report

The clinic in [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName] kept the lower levels closed while [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentOfficial] moved medicine and clean filters through one guarded hatch. Night crews now work inside a measured air column, and [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentAuthority] has a rule the shelter can inspect.

The seal around [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName] held in the clinic and food rooms, but a service shaft stayed open during the coldest shifts. The lower levels remain usable with a narrower ration and a visible debt to the filter stores.

A cracked hatch broke the seal at [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName]. The Deaths register carries the night crew losses, while [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentAuthority] must answer for an airlock that failed under the shelter's own watch.
Evo II:
The Rotating Team Report

The surface crews at [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName] changed shifts before the frost reached the intake tower. Food stores covered the handover, adaptation rose among the workers, and [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentOfficial] can keep one reclamation route open without exhausting a single crew.

The rotation at [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName] saved the strongest crews, but the food ledger could not cover every handover. The night route remains open with slower work and a memory of who was left outside the warm room.

A late rotation left the intake tower at [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName] exposed through the dark hours. The Deaths register records the crews who did not return, and [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentAuthority] faces a shelter that can no longer promise equal relief.
Evo III:
The Emergency Vent Report

Scrap crews opened controlled vents around the ash-choked rooms at [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName]. The shelter traded some warmth for clean circulation, and the recognition ledger now names the haulers who made the vent plan possible.

The vents at [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName] cleared the clinic but left the sleeping rooms in a cold draft. Reclamation gained a narrow route, while [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentOfficial] must ration warmth until the next inspection.

The emergency vent at [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName] opened into a pocket of ash. The Deaths register records the first crews at the grate, and the shelter now treats every open duct as a possible breach.
Evo IV:
The Household Ledger Report

The household ledger at [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName] assigned filters by room, age, and night duty. Recognition rose because the counts were read aloud, and [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentAuthority] can defend the ration rule before every shelter district.

The household ledger at [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName] covered the clinic and the first family rooms, but the outer bunks received thinner filters. The rule remains legible, although the shelter has marked the families who paid the largest share.

The household counts at [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName] broke down when the last filters were divided. The Deaths register carries the rooms left without cover, and [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentOfficial] must face the households that saw the ration fail.
Evo V:
The Filter Audit

The delayed audit returned to [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName] with clean counts and a working airlock. The shelter has enough filters and medicine to train another night crew, while [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentAuthority] turns the chosen policy into a standing rule.

The delayed audit at [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName] found a usable reserve, but the policy still depends on careful rationing. The clinic can train a smaller crew and the household districts have kept their own record of the missing margin.

The delayed audit at [?fallout_event_217_filters_state_id.GetName] found another breach behind the first repair. Filters and medicine have fallen below a safe reserve, the Deaths register remains open, and [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentAuthority] must carry the failure into the next shelter season.

Details: The dormitory in [?fallout_event_dispatch_issued_target.GetName] has filled beyond its winter register. Coughing has moved from the clinic beds to the cooking room, and [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentOfficial] must decide whether the room is sealed, divided, treated in public, or kept out of the public ledger. Every choice leaves a record in the state.
Evo I:
The Sealed Ward Report

The sealed dormitory in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] held through the cold shift. Filters were counted at the hatch, attendants changed in pairs, and the clinic kept its medicine away from the cooking room. Disease pressure has fallen, although every bed now carries a name and a watch.

The seal around the dormitory in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] held for the clinic and the first bunks, but a service door opened when the stove ran low. The ward is still usable, though the attendants have less medicine and a narrower shelter margin.

The seal in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] failed when the night crew crossed the dormitory without a clean filter. Fever reached the cooking room, the Deaths register carries the first losses, and [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentAuthority] must answer for the order that promised more protection than the ward possessed.
Evo II:
The Split-Bunk Report

The bunks in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] were split before the frost settled. Families carried blankets between rooms, attendants marked the clean routes, and the ward learned which households could shelter apart without abandoning the sick.

The split-bunk order in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] moved the strongest households first. Food ran short at the outer rooms, and exposure rose on the corridors, but the clinic has not lost its entire shelter list.

The bunks in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] were dispersed without enough food or warm rooms. Fever followed the corridor lights, the shelter ledger lost its order, and the Deaths register records people who were moved into cold spaces without attendants.
Evo III:
The Public Ward Report

The public ward in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] kept the clinic doors open without turning the street into a waiting room. Medicine was issued by the same tally used by the shelter officers, and the attendants learned which cases needed quiet before the next cold shift.

The public ward in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] treated the first queue, but medicine ran thin before the outer rooms were called. The public count is visible, and the shelter officers now carry a dispute over which beds received the last measured course.

The public ward in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] opened its doors before the clinic could separate the coughing rooms. Medicine was spent without lowering disease pressure, exposure rose around the queue, and the Deaths register carries the patients and attendants who waited in the open.
Evo IV:
The Concealed Fever Report

The concealed ward in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] kept its doors shut long enough to rebuild a small medicine reserve. The attendants used scrap for a second stove and told the nearest families the truth before the illness reached the market queue.

The concealed ward in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] survived the first review, but the fever did not stay inside the marked rooms. The public ledger remains incomplete, and the next attendants will inherit a shelter with less trust and a rising disease pressure.

The concealed ward in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] broke when a patient was carried through the kitchen at dawn. Fever crossed the dormitory, the Deaths register records the rooms that lost their last attendants, and [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentAuthority] must carry the concealment into every later clinic decision.
Evo V:
The Dormitory Follow-up

The follow-up in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] found a ward that could teach its rules to a second shelter. Disease pressure has eased again, the attendants have a smaller but reliable reserve, and the chosen policy now lives in the country's memory.

The follow-up in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] found a shelter that survived by exception. The ward can still treat a small wave, but the food and medicine ledgers remain tight and the people who were moved remember which door closed first.

The follow-up in [?fallout_event_256_state_id.GetName] found another fever pocket behind the dormitory stove. Disease pressure has returned, the Deaths register is open again, and [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentOfficial] must revise the shelter list before the next frost.

Details: [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentAuthority] has a death register with more entries than the shelter office can verify. Families bring scraps of paper to the cold census room, while the military archive marks entire streets as unresolved. Recognition remains low enough that the country can still choose what the public will inherit.
Evo I:
The public register reached the shelter kitchens with names, districts, and the last verified household mark. Families can challenge an entry without reopening the entire ledger, and Recognition has begun to recover.

The published register reached the market square with gaps between the Deaths ledger and the family papers. The country has a visible record, but every correction now carries a dispute over who was counted first.

The published register broke under the weight of unverified entries. Power failed in the census room, the Deaths ledger lost its cross-check, and the missing names became another source of public fear.
Evo II:
The military archive sealed the raw lists, assigned each district a custodian, and stopped duplicate claims from taking food tickets twice. The officers have a coherent record, though the public receives only verified totals.

The restricted archive kept the lists dry and powered, but the first district returns arrived without household witnesses. Recognition fell as families learned that a complete file could still remain out of reach.

The restricted archive lost its intake route when power and clerks failed together. Unverified names were folded into the military file, and the Deaths ledger records the people who waited for a confirmation that never came.
Evo III:
The community memorial rooms kept the names beside the winter ration tables. Neighbors compared family marks, volunteers corrected the first list, and the country gained a shared account of which streets had gone quiet.

The memorial rooms opened before the clerks could verify every paper. The gatherings kept the names visible, yet food and scrap ran short when two districts claimed the same shelter places.

The memorial rooms became a queue without enough heat or paper. Rival lists were read aloud as accusations, the Deaths ledger gained new entries, and the country lost the common room that had been meant to hold its memory.
Evo IV:
Local clerks carried household sheets from shelter to shelter and returned one signed list to the capital. Their work did not make the losses smaller, but it made the living legible enough for food, medicine, and a name to meet again.

Local clerks reconciled the largest shelters and left the outlying roads unresolved. The central ledger has a usable spine, while Recognition remains uneven wherever the winter patrols cannot reach.

Local clerks ran out of power and paper before the outer districts were visited. The central list contradicts the shelter rolls, families lose access to the correction desk, and the Deaths ledger records the resulting shortages.
Evo V:
The follow-up found a country that can carry its missing names into the next season. The register has a custodian, the shelter rolls share one correction route, and [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentOfficial] can answer a family without opening three separate ledgers.

The follow-up found a register that works in the capital and breaks at the edges. The names survive as contested memory, while the country must still decide which local roll will govern the next ration issue.

The follow-up found the register room without a working correction route. The Deaths ledger has reopened, families carry duplicate papers through the cold, and [ROOT.GetAirWinterGovernmentAuthority] cannot promise that the next list will be more complete.

Details: The shelter clinic has recorded a birth with a living mother, a trained attendant, and enough heat to keep the child breathing. The country must decide whether the first safe birth becomes a public register, a protected household, a civic campaign, or an elders rite.
Evo I: Public celebration result: the hall keeps the clinic record visible and links a living child to the Deaths ledger. Partial result: the birth is known in the capital while outer shelters dispute the next medicine and blanket issue. Failure result: the public hall loses heat and medicine, leaving the clinic record exposed to another night of loss.
Evo II: Private protection result: the inner door holds and the clinic marks a protected household. Partial result: the family reaches the inner room while medicine cannot cover follow-up care. Failure result: access becomes a dispute and the clinic loses a stable care schedule.
Evo III: Civic campaign result: the birth record becomes staffed work for food, power, and the next cohort. Partial result: the campaign reaches the capital and a few rail shelters. Failure result: the public count loses food, power, and confidence.
Evo IV: Elders rite result: a shared calendar and witness list carry the child into the next winter. Partial result: the name survives while medicine limits the witnesses. Failure result: the rite preserves its words while the shelter loses its common schedule.
Evo V: The 180-day callback leaves a supply route and durable witness, preserves the generation-change memory, or reopens the Deaths ledger when the clinic loses its route.

Event Name: The School in the Vent Room
Details: The first children born after the shelters sealed their doors now ask what the world was before the ash. A retired teacher has cleared a room beside the ventilation stack, and the country must choose which curriculum can survive the next ration cycle.
Evo I: Technical curriculum success: broken meters, hand tools, and a salvaged circuit board become a practical course for safe grid repair. Partial result: the children can copy a wiring diagram while dangerous repairs remain with older crews. Failure result: a damaged panel turns the lesson into a warning about teaching before the lamp is secure.
Evo II: Old-world history success: old maps sit beside the shelter register without reopening an old border. Partial result: stories survive while recognition limits leave witnesses outside the room. Failure result: the archive becomes a quarrel over which government deserves to be remembered.
Evo III: Civic survival success: water rosters, clinic notices, and repair requests become public work for a new cohort. Partial result: the class reaches the central shelter and two outer rooms. Failure result: equal duties arrive before equal food and become another ration dispute.
Evo IV: Faith classroom success: a shared calendar and quiet rite give the new cohort a language for carrying grief without closing the room to other families. Partial result: the calendar survives while medicine limits attendance. Failure result: the classroom becomes a boundary before it becomes a common shelter lesson.
Evo V: The 210-day cohort callback finds a staffed school, an uneven but real institution, or a room without a stable teacher and supply route. The education ledger and curriculum memory remain with the country after cleanup.

Details: The fever dormitory is quiet now, but its beds, drains, and cracked observation windows still occupy scarce shelter space. The country must decide whether the ward becomes a home for veterans, a research clinic, a memorial hall, or an empty room kept ready for the next emergency.
Evo I: Veteran home success: injured crews gain a staffed recovery institution with repaired beds and a public duty roster. Partial result: the home opens while medicine leaves the hardest cases in the queue. Failure result: the ward opens before its drains and supply route are ready, turning service into a public accusation.
Evo II: Research clinic success: fever records stay beside clean instruments and a working lamp. Partial result: one bench and a narrow medicine cabinet survive while outer shelters wait. Failure result: a failed test and missing medicine make private proof a public warning.
Evo III: Memorial hall success: families share one room where grief does not compete with a ration line. Partial result: the central shelter gathers names while outer families keep separate lists. Failure result: the hall becomes a contest over whose fever memory deserves the first stone.
Evo IV: Reserved empty ward success: clean visible beds remain ready for a future emergency. Partial result: some beds are open on paper while outer shelters distrust the supply route. Failure result: dust, disputed keys, and a silent medicine cabinet turn capacity into suspicion.
Evo V: The 240-day institution callback finds a staffed ward, an uneven but durable central institution, or a room without a stable keeper and supply route. Ward capacity, research, trust, and policy memory remain after cleanup.

Details: Families in the sealed shelters need a rule for partners, guardians, ration inheritance, and citizenship. The country must choose a civil code, communal contracts, congregational records, or a narrow private protection.
Evo I: Civil law success: registry clerks settle household names and guardianship across shelters. Partial result: the capital code reaches only some outer rooms. Failure result: disputed names destroy the first pages of the register.
Evo II: Communal contract success: neighborhood councils witness household agreements close to the families. Partial result: one common form gains local exceptions. Failure result: rival witnesses sign competing contracts.
Evo III: Religious authority success: congregations open shared marriage books to families from different shelter traditions. Partial result: members receive reliable records while unaligned families wait. Failure result: rival registers name competing heirs.
Evo IV: No state role success: a narrow shelter register protects household identity while private custom remains free. Partial result: families gain room to choose but uneven protection. Failure result: no common rule protects ration inheritance or guardianship.
Evo V: The 300-day household callback measures whether families can carry names, guardianship, and ration rights across shelter lines. Legitimacy, integration, fertility, exposure, and the selected law remain with the country after cleanup.

Details: The second-generation settlement has enough stored Power and Scrap to attempt a first live electrical circuit. It must choose a guarded central grid, local cooperatives, military control, or a foreign-backed relay compact, then live with the result during a long maintenance year.
Evo I: Central grid success: one control room reaches the pumps and builds durable capacity and governance. Partial: the pumps work while outer relays remain contested. Failure: synchronized start burns cabinets and weakens trust.
Evo II: Cooperative success: neighborhood crews share a public repair ledger and build resilience. Partial: local circuits work without a common standard. Failure: switching authority disputes destroy most of the network.
Evo III: Military success: guarded fuel lines and a drilled schedule return the pumps. Partial: the garrison receives dependable power while civilian districts wait. Failure: a fuel dispute leaves the main relay dark.
Evo IV: Foreign-backed success: an outside partner supplies compatible relays and a fast first current. Partial: one line works while local crews improvise adapters. Failure: incompatible coils spend Recognition without a working circuit.
Evo V: The 270-day maintenance callback tests whether the first circuit becomes a durable institution. Capacity, governance, dependency, resilience, exposure, resources, and grid memory remain with the country after cleanup.

Details: The second-generation settlement has enough stored Power and Scrap to make one district visible after dark. The country must choose whether the first dependable current serves the capital, the clinics, the factory streets, or the perimeter, then live with a 240-day public maintenance year.
Evo I: Capital first: the capital receives a shared public schedule and a durable civic face. Partial: the control room is lit while outer streets fail when the wind turns cold. Failure: the first circuit trips before the first notice is read.
Evo II: Clinics first: night wards receive the first reliable current and families can find care after sunset. Partial: the clinics hold a narrow emergency schedule. Failure: a relay fault leaves a crowded ward dark and spends medicine and trust.
Evo III: Factories first: workshops and loading bays share the first industrial current and produce tools for the unlit streets. Partial: factory lamps hold for short shifts. Failure: a feeder burns and stored food is spoiled during the restart.
Evo IV: Perimeter first: ash roads and gates receive a guarded line of lamps. Partial: the main gate is lit while side roads remain dark. Failure: a failed feeder pulls the surviving current behind the wall.
Evo V: The 240-day public maintenance callback finds a maintained city schedule, an uneven but durable public light, or a return to hand lamps. City identity, civic capacity, production, security, exposure, resources, and policy memory remain with the country after cleanup.

Details: The second-generation settlement has one sealed grain hopper beside a frozen rail spur. The country must choose whether the surviving store becomes a public granary, a guarded military depot, a licensed merchant exchange, or a visible ration center for families arriving from the ash road. The choice leads to a 210-day storehouse maintenance year.
Evo I: Public granary: the hopper count and ration rule become visible to every shelter. Partial: the central ledger works while the frozen rail edge waits. Failure: a damp seal spoils the public store before its first full count.
Evo II: Military depot: grain, fuel, and patrol routes share one guarded board. Partial: patrols receive measured loads while civilian queues wait. Failure: a fuel dispute leaves grain behind the depot gate.
Evo III: Merchant exchange: licensed carriers reopen a measured grain market and carry route news. Partial: the capital exchange works while outer roads lag. Failure: altered weights and a missing seal break the first trade.
Evo IV: Refugee ration center: arriving families receive water and grain under a visible intake rule. Partial: the main door serves the first queue while the road line waits. Failure: the center opens before its water barrels arrive and food spoils in the queue.
Evo V: The 210-day storehouse callback finds a durable public store, a guarded but uneven route, or a return to disputed ledgers. Grain capacity, logistics, market legitimacy, refugee integration, spoilage, resources, and policy memory remain with the country after cleanup.

Details: A freight warehouse survives behind locked doors and a bowed ash roof. Its boards mention medical crates, machine parts, and sealed drums, but the country cannot tell which marks mean clean stock. The chain asks whether to open the store, inspect it under quarantine, sell its coordinates through a carrier contract, or leave it sealed behind a filtered watch.
Evo I: Open immediately: salvage crews take the front racks and publish an inventory. Partial: the front bay opens while the rear floor waits. Failure: a rotten pallet spreads powder through the repair yard.
Evo II: Inspect under quarantine: a clean corridor separates medicine from sealed drums. Partial: the main racks are recovered while the last room waits. Failure: a bad mark ruins medicine and the filter tally.
Evo III: Sell the coordinates: licensed carriers buy access under public salvage law. Partial: the front racks are paid while outer crates remain disputed. Failure: the coordinates are sold twice and crates vanish.
Evo IV: Leave sealed: a fenced watch preserves a future claim. Partial: the main door is safe while the rear lane remains exposed. Failure: weather and an uncounted watch leave the seal untrusted.
Evo V: The 180-day warehouse claim callback records whether the policy created usable salvage law, a contested rear room, or a renewed contamination and trust burden. Access, salvage, contamination, legitimacy, scavenger reputation, resources, and policy memory remain with the country after cleanup.

Event Name: A Permit for the Dead City
Details: The ash-covered city still has a road wide enough for one convoy, but every map ends at the same collapsed checkpoint. The country must decide whether to send a state expedition, license salvage guilds, seize the road with soldiers, or forbid entry until the air is cleaner.
Evo I: State expedition success: a protected survey finds usable stores and marks a public route into the dead city. Partial result: the first block is mapped while the outer streets remain unsafe. Failure result: the expedition loses people and medicine at the checkpoint, and the Deaths register records the road as a failed promise.
Evo II: Licensed guilds success: carriers receive a measured permit and return with salvage under a visible contract. Partial result: the guilds recover a front warehouse while the city road remains contested. Failure result: rival crews falsify the permit, waste fuel, and leave the city more exposed than before.
Evo III: Military seizure success: soldiers secure the city road and bring back power parts under guard. Partial result: the gate holds while civilian crews wait outside the cordon. Failure result: the seizure burns fuel and trust, damages the checkpoint, and raises the city's contamination burden.
Evo IV: Forbid entry success: the country preserves shelter and filters while the dead city remains a marked exclusion. Partial result: the road is watched but the city claim stays unresolved. Failure result: an unguarded exclusion line breaks, exposure rises, and the next permit inherits a damaged memory.
Evo V: The 210-day city callback renews the permit, leaves a partial road, or abandons the claim after another contamination loss. Scrap, Medicine, Fuel, Power, Recognition, Cohesion, reclamation, supply, exposure, and state memory remain with the country after cleanup.

Details: The country finds an ash-frosted technical facility with an incomplete staff board, a ring-bound maintenance manual, and a surviving industrial or arms complex. The chosen policy freezes Power, Scrap, Medicine, Recognition, Cohesion, and one deterministic native state before a 35-day result and a 240-day maintenance callback. Failure damages a facility and routes population loss through the Deaths system.
Evo I: Follow the surviving procedure: spend Power, Scrap, and Medicine to work from the intact manual pages. Success restores guarded heat and filtered air, partial success leaves a fragile pressure gate, and failure damages the plant.
Evo II: Improvise with local tools: spend Power and Scrap to shorten the sequence. Success creates a narrow safe circuit, partial success produces intermittent heat, and failure damages a machine and moves a ward.
Evo III: Recruit an engineer from abroad: spend Power, Medicine, and Recognition for a protected specialist. Success finds a bypass, partial success identifies the fault without a control board, and failure loses the escort route.
Evo IV: Seal the facility: spend Shelter, Filters, and Scrap before ash reaches the inner rooms. Success preserves the shelter, partial success consumes maintenance stock, and failure breaks the seal in the cold.
Evo V: The delayed inspection renews the protocol, retains one service room, or abandons the facility after a second contamination burden.

Details: An automated plant survives behind an ash fence, with a relay voice repeating an old production order. The country must choose whether to integrate the machine into civil command, dismantle it for parts, let a protocol council interpret it, or isolate it behind a guarded perimeter. The selected native state carries a 49-day machine result and a 300-day inspection callback.
Evo I: Integrate the machine: spend Power, Scrap, and Recognition to place the plant under a human maintenance roster. Success brings supervised production, partial success preserves a narrow schedule, and failure damages the workshop and sends a false evacuation order.
Evo II: Dismantle it for parts: spend Scrap, Shelter, and Filters to recover drive units without opening the sealed logic cabinet. Success keeps pumps running, partial success recovers only obvious motors, and failure releases hot ash into the service yard.
Evo III: Let the protocol council interpret it: spend Medicine, Recognition, and Cohesion to give the machine a place in settlement law. Success creates a questioned civic protocol, partial success leaves families divided, and failure lets a diagnostic loop lock the plant.
Evo IV: Isolate the plant and observe: spend Power, Filters, and Medicine to map the relays behind a sealed perimeter. Success preserves a quiet reserve, partial success protects one circuit, and failure forces a ward uphill after contaminated dust escapes.
Evo V: The delayed inspection renews a supervised machine relationship, stabilizes a partial protocol, or abandons the facility after another contamination burden.

Details: A frost sealed relay room has yielded reels, shelter notices, and a working transmitter. The country must choose whether to preserve every recording, curate a civic archive, weaponize the broadcasts, or trade verified copies with foreign partners. The selected native state carries a 42-day archive result and a 270-day callback.
Evo I: Preserve every recording: the archive remains unedited and supports shared memory, research, and local supply. Partial result: damaged reels retain names and dates. Failure result: the transmitter burns the archive and the state records a public loss.
Evo II: Curate a civic archive: teachers, clerks, and station engineers verify names and dates for a legitimate public catalogue. Partial result: the catalogue opens with disputed omissions. Failure result: rival reviewers turn the archive into a new institutional grievance.
Evo III: Weaponize the broadcasts: edited testimony becomes a campaign against rival councils. Partial result: contradictory cuts win leverage while trust thins. Failure result: static and forged fragments discredit the archive and damage the relay.
Evo IV: Trade verified copies: foreign partners exchange medicine, wire, and access for certified recordings. Partial result: some bundles arrive while the route needs witnesses. Failure result: unsafe demands and a lost shipment close the exchange.
Evo V: The 270-day callback brings a trusted duplicate, a damaged copy, or a forged reel and leaves archive memory, diplomacy, legitimacy, and exposure with the country.

Details: A cooling crew has kept a nuclear reactor alive inside a state that no council can defend. The country must choose joint authority, military occupation, an engineer protectorate, or permanent shutdown. The selected native state carries a 35-day reactor result and a 240-day inspection callback.
Evo I: Joint authority: a civilian and technical board shares the cooling schedule. Partial result: pumps work but control access remains disputed. Failure result: claimant conflict leaves the reactor more exposed.
Evo II: Military occupation: troops secure the control room and restore guarded grid service. Partial result: soldiers hold the plant while cooling crews resist. Failure result: force arrives after a valve seizure and damages the protection layer.
Evo III: Engineer protectorate: the cooling crew receives protected authority and trains replacements. Partial result: the crew preserves the core while withholding parts. Failure result: a bypass fails and turns neutral safety into a political accusation.
Evo IV: Permanent shutdown: drain and seal the core for a lower-exposure future. Partial result: the spent-fuel vault still needs watch rotations. Failure result: the plant remains in dangerous low output with no trusted successor.
Evo V: The 240-day inspection returns a clean maintenance ledger, a partial alarm report, or a broken fuel record and leaves reactor memory, power, exposure, diplomacy, and the local successor institution with the country.

Details: A radar station above a thawing ridge still holds a weather log, a radio mast, and a crew that can read ash fronts before they reach the shelters. The country must decide whether the station serves civilian observers, a guarded forecast command, a shared regional warning net, or a quiet withdrawal. The selected native state carries a 42-day climate result and a 300-day station review callback.
Evo I: Fund the observers: Power, Fuel, Medicine, and Recognition keep civilian readers at the mast. Success gives the shelters a measured warning calendar and protects a local supply route. Partial success keeps one ridge forecast alive. Failure damages the radar station and sends the Deaths ledger into the weather record.
Evo II: Militarize the forecast: Power and Fuel put the station under a drilled command while Cohesion pays for the order. Success gives patrols a usable ash-front warning. Partial success protects the main road while outer districts wait. Failure turns a missed signal into a military grievance and damages the radar station.
Evo III: Share the regional records: Power, Medicine, and Recognition carry the readings to neighboring governments. Success makes the station a trusted climate exchange. Partial success sends incomplete readings beyond the border. Failure spends the contact route without a dependable forecast and leaves the station exposed.
Evo IV: Abandon the tower: Fuel, Power, and Recognition close the mast under a visible safety order. Success preserves crews and filters for another shelter. Partial success leaves a guarded instrument room. Failure loses the withdrawal route, damages the station, and increases exposure around the ridge.
World-End Scenario: The 300-day station review finds a working forecast, an uneven warning net, or a closed tower after another ash season. Forecast, contact, intelligence, exposure, supply, reclamation, and climate memory remain with the country after cleanup.

Details: An ash-covered viaduct shelters ration stalls beside a surviving rail spur. The country must decide whether the exchange serves a public price board, a depot levy, a guarded ration gate, or open barter. The selected native state carries a 35-day market result and a 270-day civic review callback.
Evo I: License the market: Food, Scrap, Medicine, and Recognition issue stall licenses and a common price board. Success brings food, supplies, and a public ration mark. Partial success leaves a second night price. Failure loses the licensing queue and damages the supply route.
Evo II: Tax the stalls for public stores: Food, Scrap, and Cohesion fund a measured levy for depots. Success fills public stores without breaking the route. Partial success leaves traders hiding part of their loads. Failure breaks the levy and turns carts away.
Evo III: Police the exchange: Scrap, Medicine, and Recognition put wardens at the scales and ration gate. Success stops hoarding while keeping merchants present. Partial success protects the main store with harsh inspections. Failure drives caravans away and damages the supply node.
Evo IV: Tolerate barter: a small Scrap, Food, and Recognition reserve leaves the arches open to informal trade. Success grows bargain routes through the rail cut. Partial success keeps stalls alive without one ration mark. Failure lets hidden hoards empty the depots.
World-End Scenario: The 270-day civic review finds a working exchange, a divided price board, or broken scales after another ash season. Food, scrap, medicine, ration, merchant, exposure, supply, reclamation, and market memory remain with the country after cleanup.

Details: An ash clinic at a freight border finds chalk, starch, and a bitter solvent inside boxes marked with the old medical seal. A river-road trader offers another shipment before the next ash wind. The country must decide whether to test the first batch in public, buy quietly, charter an apothecary guild, or seize the stock for a garrison quartermaster. The selected native state carries a 42-day medicine result and a 330-day supplier review callback.
